opening_summary: Thirty-four terms for getting a picture or a sound to work inside a Godot game, from pixels and frames to import settings, loops and the mix. With the exact term, you can tell an AI coding agent what to fix.
opening_description: 34 terms for 2D art and sound assets in Godot.

idea.narration: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Newcomers often think an image's resolution is the size the game shows it at. It is not. Resolution is only the pixels in the file. The game draws into its own viewport, and the file has to be scaled to fit it. This film goes through the terms group by group, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.
idea.text:
An image's resolution
is the size the game shows
idea.replacementWords: only the pixels in its file

beats.narration: This table is the map. Thirty-four terms in four groups, each about getting a picture or a sound to work inside the engine. The first group is size and pixels. Resolution, viewport, aspect ratio, uniform vs non-uniform, texel, nearest vs linear and integer scaling.

The second group is frames and cutouts. Sprite sheet, texture atlas, SpriteFrames, frame rate, alpha channel, transparent background, PNG vs JPEG, two image file formats, and fringe. These terms say how frames are cut from an image, and how their edges stay clean.

The third group is import, readability and collider. Import settings, lossless vs lossy, mipmaps, silhouette, readability and collider. These terms say what the engine does to a file, and what the player actually sees.

The fourth group is sound. PCM, which is raw audio samples, sample rate, Nyquist limit, procedural synthesis, WAV vs Ogg Vorbis, two sound file formats, loop point, one-shot, AudioStreamPlayer, polyphony, bus, decibel, headroom and clipping. They say how a sound is stored, looped, played and mixed.

On the left is an image file, a red circle, drawn at half size. Resolution is the width and height of an image in pixels. It is a fact about the file, not about the game. This file is one thousand twenty-four by eight hundred seventy-three, which makes eight hundred ninety-three thousand, nine hundred fifty-two pixels. For example, a picture of termite soldiers that an image model made for an enemy arrived at exactly that resolution, far bigger than the game would ever draw it.

Beside the file, at the same scale, is the red box of the Viewport, the area the game draws into. It is set in Project Settings, and the window scales it. Resolution is pixels in the file, and the viewport is pixels the game draws into. Here the file is one point six times wider and two point four two times taller. For example, the Walker game draws into a six hundred forty by three hundred sixty viewport, stretched to fill its window.

Now both rectangles are drawn the same height. Aspect ratio is width divided by height, the shape of a rectangle whatever its size. The image comes to one point one seven, nearly square. The viewport comes to one point seven eight, wide. The ratios differ, so no single scale makes the image fill the viewport exactly. For example, a title screen painted nearly square cannot fill a wide game window without bars at the sides or a stretched picture.

Two ways to shrink the file into the viewport. Uniform vs non-uniform is the choice between one scale factor on both axes and different factors that distort. On the left, two factors squash the circle into an ellipse. On the right, one factor, the smaller, zero point four one two, keeps the circle round and leaves bars at the sides. For example, a character portrait for a dialogue box should be scaled uniformly, or the face comes out stretched sideways.

This is a small invented sprite, six by six, drawn as a grid. A Texel is one pixel of a texture, counted inside the image before the engine draws it. This sprite stores thirty-six texels, and the red square marks one of them, a white texel with the value zero. For example, a coin icon stored as a tiny grid of texels still holds exactly those texels when the camera zooms in, even though each one now covers many screen pixels.

The same sprite, drawn four times larger in two ways. Nearest vs linear names two ways the engine fills screen pixels from texels. Nearest takes one texel and keeps hard edges. Linear blends four and smooths them. On the left nearest keeps two shades. On the right linear makes twenty-four, every extra one a grey the artist never drew. For example, Godot's project default is Linear, so a pixel-art enemy looks soft until its sprite node is set to Nearest.

Three rows show how wide each sprite pixel lands on screen. Integer scaling means enlarging by whole numbers, so every pixel of pixel art stays the same width. At scale two, every pixel is two screen pixels wide, and at scale three, all are three. At two point five, widths alternate, so some are fifty percent wider. For example, the Walker game stretches its viewport to a window exactly twice as wide and twice as tall, so each game pixel becomes a clean block.

One image file, cut into four equal cells of forty-eight by forty-eight pixels, each holding a bug. A Sprite sheet is one image that holds many frames in a grid. This file is one hundred ninety-two by forty-eight pixels, and because the cells are equal, a test can count them. The sprite sheet is the image, and SpriteFrames is the resource that plays it. For example, a hero's run cycle generated as one row of poses in a single PNG file is a sprite sheet.

Now the last cell is lit, and its bug is cut out below. A Texture atlas is many small images packed into one big texture, each picture a region, a rectangle of it. Godot cuts a frame as an AtlasTexture, the sheet plus that rectangle. Here the region starts one hundred forty-four pixels across and zero down, forty-eight wide and forty-eight tall. For example, the coin, heart and key icons on a game's score bar can share one atlas, each drawn from its own rectangle.

A text box lists one animation, and the bug plays beside it. SpriteFrames is a Godot resource that holds named animations, each with its frames, a speed and a loop flag. This one is named walk, plays frames zero to three at five FPS, frames per second, and loops. Five FPS is what a new animation gets by default. For example, in Walker's termite exercise the agent wrote a SpriteFrames file with one animation for each soldier, named by head colour.

The same four frames, played side by side at two speeds. Frame rate is how many frames are shown each second. At five FPS one walk cycle takes zero point eight seconds. At twelve FPS it takes zero point three three seconds. The frames are the same, and only the pace changes. For example, a beetle enemy that seems to scurry too fast can be calmed down by lowering the frame rate of its walk animation, with no new art at all.

A strip shows one pixel at nine opacities, from see-through on the left to solid on the right. The Alpha channel is the extra channel, after red, green and blue, that stores how opaque each pixel is. Zero is fully see-through, and one is fully solid. Alpha is a value stored in the file. For example, a ghost enemy drawn with its body at alpha zero point five lets the level behind it show through.

Two versions of the same dark sprite. A Transparent background means the pixels around the art really are alpha zero, a true cutout. On the left, a model asked for transparent painted a checkerboard, so the corner pixel is alpha one. On the right, the art was made on solid grey, then cut, so the corner is alpha zero. For example, Walker's own art notes say never to prompt for a transparent background, because the generator bakes in a checkerboard.

Rows of boxes show the channels each file type stores per pixel. PNG vs JPEG is the choice between a lossless file that keeps alpha and a lossy file with no alpha at all. A PNG stores red, green, blue and alpha. A JPEG stores only the first three, so its memory bar is shorter. For example, the termite reference image arrived as a JPEG with a white background, so a sprite cut straight from it would keep a white box around the creature.

Two strips sample one sprite edge over a dark red level. Fringe, or halo, is the pale rim of edge colour left around a cutout. Filtering blends in the colour stored in the see-through pixels. Stored as white, the lightest sample is zero point four four, a pale halo. With fix alpha border, an import option that stores the edge colour there, it is zero point two nine. For example, a dark enemy cut from white shows a pale outline whenever that option is off.

A chain of three boxes, your file, a text file beside it, and a cache. Import settings are the options for one asset that control how Godot converts it, kept in a text file ending in dot import, next to the source. Godot never uses your PNG or WAV directly. Commit the import file, not the dot godot cache folder. For example, because the import file is plain text, an agent's test can check that a new sprite was imported lossless with mipmaps off.

In this simulated row of twenty-four pixels, lossless vs lossy is the choice between an exact copy of every pixel and a smaller file that loses detail. The lossless row keeps every pixel, so its average error is zero. The modelled lossy row stores one average for every four pixels, and its error is zero point four. Single-pixel details go first. For example, a pixel-art bat whose eyes are single pixels should be imported Lossless, or the eyes smear into its face.

Bars show a texture of two hundred fifty-six by two hundred fifty-six and its shrunk copies. Mipmaps are pre-shrunk copies of a texture, each half the size of the last, used when it is drawn small. All nine sizes cost about thirty-three percent more memory. Drawn at a quarter size, the engine uses the sixty-four by sixty-four copy. A sprite drawn at its own size does not need them. For example, turn mipmaps on for a painted backdrop the camera zooms far out from.

An invented bug, once in colour and once filled black. A Silhouette is the outline of an object on its own. The test is to fill it black at game size and ask whether the shape still says what it is. Colour and detail are gone, and what is left is what the player notices first. For example, before accepting a generated spider enemy, fill it black and check that its legs and body still make a spider, not a blob.

The bug at three sizes, and the smallest magnified six times. Readability is how well a character can be understood in the game's real view, at its real size. Shrinking four hundred thirty-six pixels to forty-eight puts nine point zero eight source pixels into each sprite pixel, so a leg four pixels wide becomes zero point four four of a pixel, a faint smear. For example, judge a new termite enemy beside the player in the running level, not in an image viewer.

In this made-up example, a character's art, the pink box with arms, sits around a red dashed box. A Collider is the shape used for contact tests, separate from the art and sized from the body. Here it is eighteen by twenty-eight pixels, and the art reaches twelve pixels past each side. The collider counts as solid, the art is what the player sees. For example, the Walker player collides as an eighteen by twenty-eight box, while its wide mascot art reaches past it.

Now the art is flipped and the little flag points left, but the dashed box has not moved. Keep the collider a sibling of the sprite node, not its child. If it were a child, mirroring or scaling the art would change the collider too. For example, when the player turns to run left, the code flips only the sprite, and the collision box stays exactly where it was.

A spike comes in from the right. It overlaps the art for twelve pixels before it touches the collider and counts as a hit. That gap is a design choice. Art past the box is fair if it is thin or decorative, and unfair if it looks like the part that hurts. Write down why. For example, a termite enemy's box can cover only its head and body, so its thin legs and antennae brush the player without a hit.

Stems mark one cycle of a tone. PCM, pulse code modulation, is uncompressed digital audio, a plain list of numbers, one per sample, each between minus one and one. Here a four hundred forty hertz tone, at twenty-two thousand fifty samples a second, has one cycle lasting two point two seven milliseconds, and every stem is one number in the list. For example, a jump sound imported from a WAV file with compression turned off is stored as PCM.

The same tone, sampled at two rates. Sample rate is how many audio samples are stored each second. At twenty-two thousand fifty a second, one cycle gets about fifty samples and the curve is smooth. At two thousand a second it gets four and a half, a crude copy, the red zigzag. For example, Godot's generator demo fills its sound buffer at twenty-two thousand fifty samples a second, so each second of its tone is that many numbers.

A chart of the pitch heard against the pitch played, at twenty-two thousand fifty samples a second. The Nyquist limit is the highest frequency a sample rate can hold, half the rate, here eleven thousand twenty-five hertz. Above it, a pitch folds back down, so a fifteen thousand hertz tone is heard as seven thousand fifty. The sample rate counts samples, and the Nyquist limit is half of it. For example, a pickup chime synthesized above that limit plays at a wrong, lower pitch.

A line of code, its formula, and the first six values. Procedural synthesis is sound made by a formula evaluated one sample at a time, with no file and no model. Each row moves the phase on a little and takes its sine, zero, then zero point one two five one, and so on. It is not a recording and not a generative model. For example, Walker's audio generator plays a four hundred forty hertz tone this way, with no sound file at all.

A made-up waveform stands for a four second music loop, at forty-four thousand one hundred samples a second. WAV vs Ogg Vorbis is a choice of sound file. WAV suits short effects, and Ogg Vorbis suits music, speech and long sounds. Their loop settings differ. A WAV counts loop begin and end in samples, and an Ogg has only one start offset. For example, a game's jump sound ships as a WAV, and its long background song as an Ogg Vorbis file.

Markers now sit at both ends, joined by an arrow. A Loop point is where a looping sound jumps back to. For this WAV the loop mode is Forward, from sample zero to sample one hundred seventy-six thousand, three hundred ninety-nine, the last sample of the four seconds. At the end, playback jumps back to the loop begin, so the ends must match. For example, a menu song can set its loop begin after a short intro, so the intro plays only once.

Two lanes play together. One-shot means a sound plays once and stops. The music loop, set to forward, goes round again. The jump sound, with looping disabled, finishes once and stops. A one-shot ends, so its finished signal arrives, and a loop never ends, so that signal never comes. For example, in Walker's audio exercise the jump and fail sounds were meant to be one-shots, but the first try left their loop mode on detect.

Two seams, where the loop's end meets its start again. Cut part way through a cycle, the wave jumps by zero point two two of full scale, and you hear a click. Cut where the wave crosses zero, the jump is zero, and there is no click. Start and end the loop on a zero crossing, then listen across the seam three times. For example, a looping engine hum for a race car that ticks once every time round was cut off a zero crossing.

A chain from a sound file, through a player node, to the Master bus. AudioStreamPlayer is the Godot node that plays one sound stream with no position in the world, so it suits music and interface sounds. Calling play sends the stream on to a bus. AudioStreamPlayer2D pans and fades with position instead. For example, a menu's button sound belongs on a plain AudioStreamPlayer, while a waterfall that grows louder as the player walks near belongs on AudioStreamPlayer2D.

A timeline of three play calls, forty milliseconds apart, on a sixty millisecond click. Polyphony is how many copies of one sound can play at once, and Godot's default is one. With one voice, each new play cuts off the last, so you hear forty, forty, then sixty milliseconds, a stutter. For example, a coin sound on a single-voice player cuts itself short when the player grabs three coins in quick succession.

Now the player is allowed four voices. Each sound is heard in full, sixty milliseconds, and neighbours overlap by twenty. There is a second fix, in the event rather than the file. Play the sound only on the transition into a state, not on every frame the state is true. For example, the rhythm game's hit sound player is set to four voices, so fast Perfect and Good hits each play whole.

Two players feed two buses, which feed Master. A Bus is a channel that sounds are routed through for shared volume and effects. Each bus can be lowered, ducked or muted on its own, so levels are set in the mix, not the file. Here the music player sits at minus twelve decibels on bus Music, and the effects player at zero on bus SFX, for sound effects. For example, a settings menu's music slider lowers the Music bus and leaves the jumps alone.

A ladder of decibel values beside their amplitudes. A Decibel is a logarithmic unit of loudness. Every minus six decibels about halves the amplitude, so minus six is zero point five zero one, minus twenty is zero point one, and minus sixty is zero point zero zero one. The scale stays short. For example, the rhythm game sets its song player to minus twelve decibels, zero point two five one of full amplitude.

A sine wave sits under a line marked maximum level, one point zero. Headroom is the spare level left between a sound's peak and the maximum. This peak is zero point five, which is minus six point zero two decibels, so the headroom is six point zero two decibels. That space is kept for loud moments. For example, a mix that leaves headroom lets an explosion land on top of the music without reaching the maximum.

The same sine, turned up by seven point six decibels. Clipping is the distortion when a signal goes past the maximum level. The peak would reach one point two, so the tops are cut flat, here on thirty-seven point two percent of the samples, and you hear a crackle. Headroom is level left below the maximum, and clipping is level past it. For example, a boss roar boosted on a bus that is already loud loses its peaks and crackles through the speakers.

Each pair sets two look-alike terms side by side. Resolution is the pixels in the image file, here one thousand twenty-four by eight hundred seventy-three. The viewport is the pixels the game draws into, six hundred forty by three hundred sixty.

Mipmaps are pre-shrunk copies of one texture, chosen by how big it appears on screen, here four sizes. Filtering is how one sample is taken from a texture, nearest or linear. Linear blends four texels.

Sample rate counts audio samples per second, twenty-two thousand fifty, too many to draw. Frame rate counts animation frames per second, five here, and every one is visible. One belongs to sound, the other to pictures.
A Loop point is where playback jumps back to, so the sound goes round again. A One-shot plays once and stops. Background music loops, and a jump sound is a one-shot.

On the left, a vague request above the exact instruction that replaces it. Make the art fit the game becomes, scale the image by one factor, zero point four one two on both axes. Two factors stretch it one point five two to one. One factor keeps the shape.

Make the pixels crisp becomes, set the filter to Nearest on the sprite node, and import Lossless with mipmaps off. After enlarging four times, linear shows twenty-four shades and nearest only two. Nearest adds no new colours.
The walk is too fast becomes, set the walk animation in SpriteFrames from twelve to six FPS. One four-frame cycle then takes zero point six seven seconds. Cycle time is frames divided by FPS.

Make the music loop becomes, import the music loop file with Loop Mode Forward, begin zero, end one hundred seventy-six thousand, three hundred ninety-nine, cut on a zero crossing. Both ends sit on zero, so there is no click.
The effect is too loud and crackles becomes, lower the SFX bus by six decibels. A peak of one point two becomes zero point six, under the maximum of one, and nothing clips.
This is a checklist of six questions to ask before a generated asset goes into the game. First, is the image scaled by one factor to the viewport, with its shape kept?
Second, is the background alpha zero at the corners, with no halo and no painted checkerboard? Check the corner pixels themselves, not a thumbnail.
Third, is the filter Nearest on the node, with mipmaps off and a Lossless import? The filter belongs to the node, and the other two belong to the import file.
Fourth, do the frame count, the layout and the speed match the SpriteFrames? A test can count frames, but only you can tell a new pose from a different creature.
Fifth, is the collider sized from the body, and kept as a sibling of the sprite, so that flipping the art never moves it?
Sixth, is the sound imported with the right loop mode, played once per event, at a safe level? Then say it exactly. Not make it crisp, but Nearest on the node, Lossless, no mipmaps.

recap_lines: Resolution is pixels in the file, the viewport is pixels the game draws into.
Pixel art needs Nearest on the node and whole-number scaling.
A sprite sheet is the image, and SpriteFrames is the resource that plays it.
Cut the background to alpha zero, and never prompt for a transparent one.
The collider is sized from the body and kept apart from the art.
A loop point repeats, a one-shot stops, and headroom keeps a mix from clipping.

your_turn.command: Give me short cases from making a two D game, one at a time, about its art and sound. Each case should turn on one of these terms, resolution, viewport, nearest vs linear, sprite sheet, SpriteFrames, mipmaps, loop point, one-shot, headroom or clipping. I must name the exact term and say why its look-alike is wrong. Wait for my reply before you give the answer.
checks: Check: each case is a game-making situation, and the answer waits for you.
Check: you named the exact term and said why its look-alike was wrong.

deck_problems: Slide 2 step 3: the two ratio labels run into each other with no gap, so the screen shows 'image: 1024 ÷ 873 = 1.17viewport: 640 ÷ 360 = 1.78'. The same label writes 1024 with no comma, where the rest of the deck writes 1,024.

Slide 7 step 2: the caption 'under one pixel: drawn at 44% strength, a faint smear' is true only if the shrink averages pixels. The course's own worked run resampled with nearest-neighbour and found the legs and antennae became broken dots, not a faint smear. Also the heading says the bugs are 'DRAWN AT HALF SIZE', but the '48 px, magnified ×6' bug is drawn about 288 px tall, which is ×6 at full size, not at the half-size scale of the others.
Slide 9 step 2: the caption says '2,000 a second gives about 4' while the label above it says '4.5 samples per cycle'. The narration says four and a half.
Slide 11 step 1: a stray pink dot is left between the 'Master bus' box and the caption at the end of the step (the moving signal dot stops outside the chain).
Slide 12 step 3: 'peak 0.50 = -6.02 dB' uses an ASCII hyphen where every other negative decibel value in the deck uses the minus sign '−'.

Slide 4: in renderSheet the four 'walk' frames differ only by a 3-pixel vertical bob, so the walk animation plays as a bounce in place. Step 4's heading says 'REAL TIME, 2 S' but the tick rows show one second of frames (5 and 12 ticks).

Slide 6 carries the badge 'Simulation' for the whole slide, but only the lossy row in step 2 is modelled; the import lines in step 1 are from Chapter 2 and the mipmap sizes in step 3 are exact arithmetic.
Naming: the map lists 'fringe' where the slide says 'Fringe (halo)', and pair 2 on the look-alike slide introduces 'Filtering', which is not one of the 34 map terms (the map has 'nearest vs linear').
